title: Job Wishes He Had Never Been Born
overview: Job breaks his silence with a raw lament, wishing he had never been born and asking why life is given to people who suffer.

parts.label: Job breaks his silence (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: After seven days sitting in silence with his friends (2:13), Job finally speaks and curses the day he was born. He does not curse God, which is what the accuser in chapters 1 and 2 said he would do.

parts.label: Unmaking his birthday (vv. 3-7)
parts.note: Job wishes the day of his birth and the night of his conception could sink into darkness and drop off the calendar. Many scholars hear v. 4, where Job asks for that day to become darkness, as God's 'let there be light' from Genesis 1 turned upside down, as if Job wants his own small piece of creation undone.

parts.label: Calling in the curse makers (vv. 8-10)
parts.note: Job calls on those who curse days, people bold enough to rouse Leviathan, a sea monster that stood for chaos in ancient stories, though scholars are unsure what practice v. 8 has in mind. He wants that night never to see dawn, because it did not shut his mother's womb and spare him this trouble (v. 10).

parts.label: Better to have died at birth (vv. 11-19)
parts.note: Job asks why he did not die as a newborn or come stillborn, and why there were knees to receive him (v. 12), probably the custom of taking a newborn onto the lap as one's own. He pictures the grave as quiet rest, where kings and slaves, the wicked and the worn out lie side by side and no one shouts orders anymore.

parts.label: Why give life to the suffering? (vv. 20-23)
parts.note: Job widens the question: why is life given to people who long for a death that will not come, and to a man whose way is hidden and whom God has hedged in? The picture in v. 23 is of a traveler with no path and no way out, and many readers hear a bitter echo of the protective hedge around Job in 1:10, though the Hebrew verbs are different.

parts.label: No rest at all (vv. 24-26)
parts.note: His sighs come with his meals and his groans pour out like water (v. 24), and what he dreaded has come (v. 25). Translations differ on the tense of v. 25, and readers differ on whether he means fears he carried in his good years or each new blow as the losses came, but he ends with no peace and no rest (v. 26). Job says his wish out loud instead of keeping it hidden, and the book does not end here. If you share his wish tonight, please tell someone you trust or call a crisis line.

disagreement: Christians differ on how to judge this speech: many traditional readers see it as impatience and a real failing on Job's part, while many others read it as honest lament that God accepts, pointing to 42:7, where God says Job spoke rightly about him.
think: When someone in deep pain says they wish they had never been born, what kind of response do you think actually helps them?
